---
title: "Group heterogeneity and marginal dispersion"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

The [paired Poisson model](poisson-mixed-models.qmd) supplied one source of structured count variation: persistent differences across aligned passage pairs. If we combine low rate and high rate pairs under one mean, the resulting counts can vary more than a Poisson distribution with that single mean would predict. We will call that across-pair increase **marginal dispersion**.

The [group deviation model](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd) assigns each pair an unobserved deviation. Conditional [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) applies after it is given, and [residuals](residuals.qmd) are then observed minus fitted count discrepancies. A marginal expectation averages over the deviation distribution. Recall that the [expectation of a function](../random-variables-and-distributions/expectation-of-functions.qmd) weights each possible deviation by its probability; applying that operation here creates the extra variance term below.

We first inspect the observed rate variation across aligned passage pairs, then state the conditional Poisson claim, average over the pair distribution, substitute fitted variation, and check which dispersion remains after conditioning.

```{r}
#| label: plot-observed-ucca-pair-rates
library(ggplot2)

ucca_rate_preview <- read.csv(
  "data/ucca-french-english/passage-counts.csv"
)
ucca_rate_preview$scene_rate <- with(
  ucca_rate_preview,
  scene_count / word_count
)

summary(ucca_rate_preview$scene_rate)

ggplot(
  ucca_rate_preview,
  aes(x = language, y = scene_rate, group = pair_id)
) +
  geom_line(color = "grey75", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_point(color = "#1F5A85", size = 1.3) +
  labs(x = "Language side", y = "Observed Scenes per word") +
  theme_classic()
```

Each line joins the English and French sides of one observed passage pair. The vertical spread across lines shows that conditional rates differ across pairs. When we average over that variation, total count variance must include both the Poisson variation within a given rate and variation in the rates themselves.

The **law of total variance** names this decomposition: total variance equals the average conditional variance plus the variance of the conditional means. Recall the same decomposition from [predictive distributions](../statistical-inference/predictive-distributions.qmd).

## Beginning with the conditional Poisson claim

For language side $l$ of passage pair $p$, write

$$
Y_{pl}\mid b_p
\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_{pl}(b_p)),
$$

with

$$
\lambda_{pl}(b_p)
=\lambda_{pl}^{(0)}\exp(b_p),
$$

where

$$
\lambda_{pl}^{(0)}
=W_{pl}\exp\left(
\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{French}_{pl}
\right)
$$

is the expected count when the pair deviation is zero, and

$$
b_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2).
$$

Conditional on a particular pair effect,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}\mid b_p]
=\mathbb{E}[Y_{pl}\mid b_p]
=\lambda_{pl}(b_p).
$$

Thus the model remains conditionally Poisson.

## Averaging over the passage-pair population

For a new aligned pair, the marginal mean is

$$
m_{pl}
=\operatorname{E}_{b}\left[\lambda_{pl}(b)\right].
$$

Recall that a [moment generating function](response-transformations.qmd) is the expectation $M_B(t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{tB}]$. It collects the expectations of powers of a random variable in a form that is convenient for calculations. Because $B\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2)$, this function is $M_B(t)=\exp(t^2\tau_p^2/2)$. Evaluating it at one and two gives the lognormal moments needed below:

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_B(t)&=\exp(t^2\tau_p^2/2),\\
\mathbb{E}[e^B]&=M_B(1)=e^{\tau_p^2/2},\\
\mathbb{E}[e^{2B}]&=M_B(2)=e^{2\tau_p^2},\\
\operatorname{Var}[e^B]&=e^{2\tau_p^2}-e^{\tau_p^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

so

$$
m_{pl}
=\lambda_{pl}^{(0)}
\exp\left(\frac{\tau_p^2}{2}\right).
$$

The law of total variance gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}]
&=\operatorname{E}_{b}
  [\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}\mid b]]
  +\operatorname{Var}_{b}
  [\mathbb{E}[Y_{pl}\mid b]]\\
&=\operatorname{E}_{b}[\lambda_{pl}(b)]
  +\operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{pl}(b)]\\
&=m_{pl}+\operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{pl}(b)].
\end{aligned}
$$

The lognormal moment identity yields

$$
\operatorname{Var}_{b}[\lambda_{pl}(b)]
=m_{pl}^2\left[\exp(\tau_p^2)-1\right].
$$

Thus,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}]
=m_{pl}
+m_{pl}^2\left[\exp(\tau_p^2)-1\right].
$$

If $\tau_p^2>0$, the second term is positive. Marginal variance then exceeds marginal mean even though every conditional count distribution is Poisson.

Setting $\tau_p=0$ collapses $B$ to zero, removes the second term, and recovers the Poisson equality $\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{pl}]=\lambda_{pl}^{(0)}$.

## Substituting the fitted UCCA pair variance

We will also compute a [**Pearson residual**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234) for each row. For a Poisson mean $\widehat\lambda_i$, this residual divides observed minus fitted count by the model's conditional standard deviation:

$$
r_i^{(P)}=\frac{y_i-\widehat\lambda_i}{\sqrt{\widehat\lambda_i}}.
$$

Squaring and summing these standardized discrepancies gives a rough conditional dispersion check. Dividing by a degrees of freedom count produces the Pearson ratio used below; because partially pooled group deviations consume information gradually, that denominator will only be a heuristic in this mixed model.

The moment calculations above describe what the fitted model implies; they do
not replace the likelihood used to estimate its parameters. The call below
refits the same [paired Poisson marginal
likelihood](poisson-mixed-models.qmd#fitting-the-paired-ucca-model). Thus
`nAGQ = 1` asks for a Laplace approximation to the integral over each pair
deviation, and `bobyqa` searches over the population coefficients and pair
standard deviation. We then use the resulting fit to inspect conditional
residuals.

```{r}
#| label: ucca-marginal-dispersion
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

ucca <- read.csv("data/ucca-french-english/passage-counts.csv")
ucca$pair_id <- factor(ucca$pair_id)
ucca$language <- factor(
  ucca$language,
  levels = c("en", "fr")
)

fit <- glmer(
  scene_count ~ language +
    offset(log(word_count)) +
    (1 | pair_id),
  data = ucca,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  nAGQ = 1L,
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

variance_table <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit))
pair_variance <- variance_table$vcov[
  variance_table$grp == "pair_id" & is.na(variance_table$var2)
]

english_passages <- ucca[ucca$language == "en", ]
reference_index <- which.min(abs(
  english_passages$word_count - median(english_passages$word_count)
))
reference_word_count <- english_passages$word_count[[reference_index]]
reference_passage <- data.frame(
  language = factor("en", levels = levels(ucca$language)),
  word_count = reference_word_count
)
conditional_mean <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = reference_passage,
  re.form = NA,
  type = "response"
)
marginal_mean <- conditional_mean * exp(pair_variance / 2)
marginal_variance <- marginal_mean +
  marginal_mean^2 * (exp(pair_variance) - 1)

pearson_residual <- residuals(fit, type = "pearson")
pearson_degrees_of_freedom <-
  nrow(ucca) - length(fixef(fit)) - 1L
conditional_pearson_ratio <-
  sum(pearson_residual^2) / pearson_degrees_of_freedom

dispersion_summary <- c(
  pair_intercept_variance = pair_variance,
  reference_english_word_count = reference_word_count,
  conditional_mean_at_reference_exposure = conditional_mean,
  marginal_mean_at_reference_exposure = marginal_mean,
  marginal_variance_at_reference_exposure = marginal_variance,
  marginal_variance_mean_ratio = marginal_variance / marginal_mean,
  conditional_pearson_ratio = conditional_pearson_ratio
)
dispersion_summary
```

The denominator subtracts the population coefficient count and one fitted variance parameter. In a GLMM, however, partially pooled group deviations consume information gradually rather than exactly one degree of freedom per parameter or group. We therefore use the Pearson ratio as a heuristic residual diagnostic and do not attach an exact chi-squared reference distribution to it.

At the observed data fit, an English passage with `r reference_word_count` annotated words has population center mean `r sprintf("%.2f", conditional_mean)` Scenes. This exposure comes from the observed English passage closest to the sample median word count. Averaging over new passage pair variation raises the mean to `r sprintf("%.2f", marginal_mean)` and gives marginal variance `r sprintf("%.2f", marginal_variance)`. The resulting marginal variance to mean ratio is `r sprintf("%.3f", marginal_variance / marginal_mean)`.

These values are computed from the fitted Poisson lognormal model at an exposure observed in the passage table.

## Diagnosing conditional fit

The marginal moment identity does not tell us whether the conditional Poisson variance fits the residual pattern under the fitted model. A Pearson diagnostic assesses that different question.

```{r}
#| label: plot-ucca-dispersion
diagnostic_data <- data.frame(
  fitted_count = fitted(fit),
  pearson_residual = pearson_residual,
  language = ucca$language
)

ggplot(
  diagnostic_data,
  aes(
    x = fitted_count,
    y = pearson_residual,
    shape = language
  )
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, color = "#1F5A85") +
  labs(
    x = "Conditional fitted Scene count",
    y = "Pearson residual",
    shape = "Language"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The conditional Pearson ratio is `r sprintf("%.3f", conditional_pearson_ratio)`, which is below one. These data are conditionally underdispersed relative to the fitted Poisson working model even though the pair intercept induces extra-Poisson *marginal* variance. The two claims refer to different conditioning levels and can hold simultaneously.

Two sides of the same passage pair share $b_p$. After that effect is averaged out, a high count on one side provides information that the pair has a high baseline, which in turn raises the expectation for the other side. A negative-binomial or observation-level dispersion term can change count variance but does not by itself encode this paired association.

| Quantity | Poisson-lognormal claim | What it describes |
|---|---|---|
| Conditional variance | $\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}\mid b_p]=\lambda_{pl}(b_p)$ | count variation at a fixed pair deviation |
| Marginal variance | $m_{pl}+m_{pl}^2[e^{\tau_p^2}-1]$ | variation across new pairs and counts |
| Cross-row covariance | positive for the two sides sharing $b_p$ | paired dependence after the effect is averaged out |

Random intercepts thus do not repair every dispersion pattern. They are licensed by a known repeated unit and explain one structured source of variation. Remaining conditional underdispersion, omitted predictors, varying associations, or another response family require separate model criticism.

## Recap and check

1. Can conditional Poisson variance coexist with marginal overdispersion? Yes. Averaging over pair heterogeneity adds the second total-variance term.
2. Does extra marginal variance imply independent rows? No. A shared pair effect also induces cross-row covariance.
3. Is the printed Pearson denominator exact for this GLMM? No. It is a declared heuristic because random effects use fractional effective information.

The tools for [model criticism and prediction](../model-criticism-and-prediction/) separate checks of conditional fit, predictive calibration, and dependence.
